title: Gullak Season 5 Is Streaming Now. The Mishra Family Got Wi-Fi, a New Annu Bhaiya, and an Identity Crisis That Feels Like Yours.
excerpt: India's first web series to return for a fifth season proves that the most revolutionary thing on Indian OTT is still a middle-class family arguing about a housing loan.
body:
There is a specific kind of comfort that only **Gullak** knows how to deliver. Not the performative warmth of a Netflix self-care drama, not the manufactured nostalgia of a heritage brand ad. This is the real thing — the sound of a pressure cooker in a cramped kitchen, a father who dreams bigger than his bank balance allows, a mother whose sacrifices are so constant they've become invisible even to her. Five seasons in, the Mishra family still feels less like fiction and more like the people you grew up around. That is the magic. And increasingly, the problem.

**Gullak Season 5**, now streaming on **SonyLIV**, is the first Indian web series ever to return for a fifth season. That milestone alone tells you something about what TVF has built here. This isn't a franchise sustained by spectacle or star power — there are no action sequences, no A-list cameos, no plot twists designed to trend on X. There is just a family, navigating the ordinary catastrophe of everyday life with the kind of specificity that makes you pause the episode to call your parents.

The season opens with the Mishra household undergoing a literal renovation — fresh paint on the walls, a new Wi-Fi router humming in the corner. **Santosh Mishra** (the peerless **Jameel Khan**) is pursuing the middle-class holy grail: a government-subsidized flat, complete with the housing loan application that will consume his every waking thought. **Shanti** (**Geetanjali Kulkarni**, still the emotional backbone of this show) is confronted with a decision about her maternal home that dredges up questions about identity and sacrifice she's spent decades burying.

Meanwhile, the sons are making choices that will ripple through the family. **Aman** (**Harsh Mayar**) has discovered a side hustle as an online astrologer — dispensing dubious cosmic advice to strangers on the internet, inevitably landing himself in trouble. And then there's the elephant in the Mishra living room: Annu Bhaiya.

> "He doesn't try to imitate the earlier Annu Bhaiya. He brings a fresh flavour and approach." — Bollywood Shaadis review

**Anant V. Joshi** steps into the role vacated by **Vaibhav Raj Gupta**, and the recasting is the one question every returning viewer needs answered. The good news: Joshi doesn't attempt an impression. He finds his own rhythm — quieter, perhaps a shade more restrained — while preserving the essential Annu-ness that fans love: the simmering frustration, the reluctant responsibility, the way he communicates entire paragraphs of emotion through a single exhale. By the third episode, you stop comparing. By the finale, you accept him.

The additions bring their own energy. **Gopal Dutt** arrives as Pinky Mama with an offer that throws the family into chaos, and **Sunita Rajwar's** Bittu Ki Mummy has evolved from nosy neighbour to full-blown social media activist and *mahila mandal* president — a characterization that is both hilarious and uncomfortably accurate. **Helly Shah** joins the ensemble as Dr. Priti, adding a new dimension to Annu's arc.

Critics have been largely warm. **Filmfare** gave it 3.5 out of 5, calling it "one of the most authentic and emotionally resonant shows produced in India." **MensXP** noted that the finale left them "emotional, teary-eyed, and deeply satisfied." **India Forums** offered a more measured take, giving it 3 out of 5 and noting that the show's greatest strength — its familiarity — is also becoming its biggest challenge. The ending, several reviewers agreed, wraps up a touch too neatly.

That criticism is fair, and it's the kind of criticism only a beloved show invites. Nobody dissects the ending of a series they don't care about. Gullak earns its scrutiny because it has earned something rarer — genuine affection.

**For the diaspora**, this is essential viewing. Gullak has always been the show you recommend to friends who ask what Indian families are really like — not the Karan Johar fantasy, not the crime-thriller grit, but the texture of a life measured in EMIs, neighborhood politics, and the quiet heroism of showing up every day. SonyLIV is available internationally, and all episodes of Season 5 are dropping weekly — the first two are already live, with Episode 3 arriving June 12.

Five seasons. Seven episodes each. No guns, no car chases, no universe-building. Just a family, a gullak on the shelf, and the stubborn belief that ordinary stories deserve extraordinary telling. The Mishras aren't going anywhere. And that's exactly the point.
author: Diaspora Desk
